newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - German shares lead European gains, dlr firm.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German shares lead European gains, dlr firm.

text.p: European bourses opened higher on Monday, led by record-high German shares as the strong U.S. dollar continued to boost exporting firms.

The dollar climbed above New York's high to reach a six-year peak against the mark in early European trading after Austrian National Bank General Director Adolf Wala said he expected the dollar to reach 1.80.
"The current development of the dollar/mark is actually an adjustment to real consumer spending parity," Wala said. "I expect (dollar/mark) to find its level at 1.80."
The dollar also strengthened as the mark continued to weaken against sterling. Sterling extended gains above 3.0235 marks, the highest level since autumn 1990, at midmorning.
Traders said continued dollar strength will help make more European exports cheaper abroad and lift exporters' profits.

"What we've seen (in German stocks) so far is perfectly justified with the dollar at this level," a Frankfurt dealer said when Germany's IBIS DAX index hurdled 4,100 points to hit an all-time high of 4,121.79 in pre-bourse, electronic trade.
The IBIS DAX's surge helped lift German shares at the start of bourse trading to a record high 4,119.84.

Leading German shares included dollar-sensitive, engineering and car stocks. Drugs group Schering AG was up 3.70 marks at 199.00, a year high at 0905 GMT, and engineering firm Siemens AG was up 2.35 at 114.95, just off its year high of 115.45 hit earlier in the session.
Swiss shares opened more than a percentage point higher, also helped by the firm dollar.
Winterthur Schweizerische Versicherungs-Gesellschaft jumped 45 Swiss francs, or 3.17 percent, at the opening to 1,463 on merger or takeover speculation.
But in London, sterling's surge overshadowed any benefits stocks would reap from the dollar's gains.
Sterling was buoyed by expectations of more British rate rises after the Bank of England raised the base rate 25 basis points on Thursday.
"People will be dwelling on sterling's rise over three marks," an equity salesman in London said.

Britain's larger-than-expected 0.8-percent drop in seasonally-adjusted June input prices helped temporarily allay fears the Bank of England would have to raise interest rates aggressively to stem inflation, which provided stocks with early underlying support.
But economists still only considered the figure as in line with forecasts because it confirmed tame inflation expectations.

"The figures are very much in line right across the board," said Peter Osler, GNI economist. "The markets have hardly done anything. They've (the data) confirmed the inflationary pressures at this part of the chain are very subdued."
British government debt, used as a gauge of long-term interest rates, was also little moved on the data, barely inching up into positive ground.
Paris markets were closed for the Bastille Day holiday.
CURRENCIES AT 1000 GMT
The dollar was at 113.95 yen and 1.7927 marks versus 113.85 and 1.7705 in late European trade on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1000 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was up 24.6 points at 4824.1.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was up 83.24 points at 4,124.21.
PARIS - The CAC-40 closed up 12.50 points at 2,941.59 on Friday.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $321.35, up from $320.05 an ounce at Friday's close. Silver was at $4.37, down two cents from Friday's close.
